chunks: How you debug software. The question: How do you debug software?
Debugging software uses the same loop as debugging hardware: make it fail on demand, read the evidence, narrow down where it goes wrong, change one thing at a time, and prove the fix.
On a microcontroller you add tools like a debugger probe and a spare pin you toggle to watch timing on a scope.
Imagine a water leak somewhere in a house. You shut the valve to half the house. If the leak continues, it is in that half, and you split again.
Debugging does the same with code: you split the search each time, instead of poking at random. One caution: unlike a valve, a print or breakpoint can change the bug itself.
The software loop. Bisect applies when a known-good version exists; otherwise you localize by state inspection. The end is always a regression test.
Breakpoint: a stop at a chosen line of code so you can inspect the state. Watchpoint: a stop whenever a chosen variable is read or written. Good for "who changes this?"
git bisect: a version-control tool that finds the first bad change by repeatedly testing the middle of a range.
Interrupt service routine (ISR): a short function the hardware runs when an event occurs.
Observer effect: when watching a bug changes it, for example because a print slows the code.
A program worked last month and now fails. There are 1000 changes since then. Test the middle one. If it fails, the bug is in the first half.
Each test halves the range, so about log 2 1000 equals 10 builds find the first bad change. For timing, set a spare pin high at the start of an ISR and low at the end.
A scope shows a 12 microseconds pulse every 1 milliseconds. The ISR uses 12 over 1000 equals 1. 2 % of the processor.
Printing a 40-character line at 115200 baud (bits per second) takes about 3. 5 milliseconds, which could hide a timing bug. That is the whole idea.
"I use the same loop as hardware: reproduce the bug, read the evidence like logs and fault registers, then localize with a debugger, watchpoints, assertions and git bisect.
On an embedded target I toggle a GPIO and watch it on a scope for timing, decode hard faults from the stacked PC, and check stack overflow, ISR races and volatile.
I watch for observer effects like printf changing the timing, and I add a regression test after the fix."
Quick check. A variable is being overwritten by unknown code. Which debugger feature finds the culprit most directly?
